newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian shares plunge as Congress withdrawal shocks.
newsitem.headline: Indian shares plunge as Congress withdrawal shocks.

text.p: The Congress Party's sudden withdrawal of crucial support to India's ruling coalition government pulled stocks sharply lower in off-market kerb deals on Sunday, brokers said.
The Congress said it was formally staking a bid to form a new federal government.
Shocked analysts said share prices across the country were likely to go into a tailspin this week.
Shares of largest private firm Reliance Industries were trading at 275 rupees in kerb deals, 10 rupees lower than the official close on the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) on Friday.
"This is something totally unexpected," said Ravi Gopalakrishan, head of sales at UBS Securities. "There's trouble ahead that doesn't look like it will be easily resolved."
Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's minority United Front alliance controls some 178 deputies in the 545-member Lok Sabha or lower house. The Congress has 142 deputies.
Shares of the country's biggest commercial bank State Bank of India fell to 295 rupees in kerb deals against the last official close of 303 rupees on the BSE.
It was not immediately clear if the Congress decision meant the shaky nine-month-old government led by Deve Gowda would have to resign and call a snap mid-term poll.
Congress officials said the withdrawal decision followed "attempts by the United Front" to split the Congress party in the key north Indian state of Uttar Pradesh.
"This is compeletely unanticipated," said the chief dealer at a UK-based brokerage. "I wouldn't be surprised if we see the index drop 200-300 points."
Bombay's benchmark stocks index closed 72.05 points, or 1.9 percent lower, at 3663.53 on Friday.
"People will unwind positions and short sellers will jump on," said UBS's Gopalakrishnan.
Iain Allison, country head at Caspian Securities, said the BSE's index was likely to fall back to near 3200 points.
"Investors are going to throw their hands up in exasperation," Allison said.
Analysts said the Congress decision was bound to affect budget proposals, announced by the United Front last month.
"The budget proposals could fall flat on their face," said an analyst at a foreign institutional investor.

In the annual budget for 1997/98 (April-March), Finance Minister P. Chidambaram announced sweeping cuts in corporate and personal taxes. The proposals are scheduled to be passed by parliament in the ongoing session.
Dealers said they were surprised that Congress weas ready to gamble on a power struggle.
"The whole mood was that the Congress wouldn't be in the shape to do anything yet. It's political suicide for the Congress," the chief dealer said.
